content: This manual defines an unexpected substance, material, or mixture that may occur in a technical or formulated pesticide. This is also referred to as an impurity. A cream refers to an opaque layer that accumulates at the top or bottom of an emulsion. The term g represents grams per milliliter at a temperature of 20 ± 2°C, incorporated into the bulk material.g., by tapping) is used to achieve density. A device, as defined in this manual, is any physical or mechanical entity preloaded with a pesticide quantity, ready for immediate use without requiring dilution or mixing. Appendix C provides a glossary of terms, including definitions of pesticide formulation types, which are detailed in Appendix E alongside the CropLife International two-letter coding system. Dispersibility describes the ease with which an insoluble solid or liquid material can be uniformly dispersed in a liquid. Dust refers to fine solid particles, potentially airborne, with a size of less than 50 µm. The European List of Notified Chemical Substances (ELINCS) and the European Inventory of Existing Commercial Chemical Substances (EINECS) numbers are identifiers for new and existing chemicals, respectively. Equivalence is defined by the FAO/WHO International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management as the determination of the similarity in impurity and toxicological profiles, as well as physical and chemical properties, of technical materials from different manufacturers. The Joint Meeting on Pesticide Specifications (JMPS) evaluates equivalence by comparing impurity and toxicological profiles, manufacturing specifications, and physical/chemical data of technical-grade active ingredients (TC/TK) from different sources. If the materials meet common specifications and pose no greater risk than the reference material, they are considered equivalent. Pesticide formulations are deemed equivalent if prepared from equivalent TC/TKs and conform to the same specifications. However, equivalence does not guarantee identical efficacy or risk profiles in specific applications. An evaluator is an expert assigned by FAO/WHO to assess data supporting a proposed specification or its extension, following the procedural principles outlined in this manual. The FAO (Food and Agriculture Organization) and WHO (World Health Organization) publish international quality standards for pesticides, known as FAO/WHO specifications. These standards are supported by data packages submitted by manufacturers or interested parties. A filler is an inert solid used as a diluent in formulations. Fines refer to undersized particles, while flammable materials are readily ignitable. A flammable liquid has a flash point between 21°C and 55°C, while a highly flammable liquid has a flash point below 21°C. Flash point is the lowest temperature at which a material forms a flammable vapor/air mixture under standard conditions. Flocculation refers to the aggregation of particles suspended in a liquid. Flowability describes the ability of materials to flow freely under specified conditions. A formulant is any substance, other than the active ingredient, intentionally included in a formulation. Formulation refers to the combination of ingredients designed to make a product effective for its intended use and application method. Friability is the tendency of a solid, such as a granule or tablet, to disintegrate by crumbling. Hazard refers to the inherent property of an agent or situation to cause adverse effects when an organism or system is exposed. Risk is the probability of an adverse effect occurring under specific circumstances. A relevant impurity is a by-product of pesticide manufacture or storage that is toxicologically significant to health or the environment, phytotoxic to treated plants, or affects pesticide stability. Water or insoluble material may also be relevant impurities if they impact stability or application. Validation is the process of establishing the reliability and relevance of a method or approach for a defined purpose. Peer validation involves independent laboratories verifying analytical methods. Pesticide refers to any chemical or biological substance or mixture intended to repel, destroy, or control pests or regulate plant growth. This includes substances used as insect or plant growth regulators, defoliants, desiccants, or agents for fruit thinning or preservation. Pesticides also encompass synergists and safeners integral to their performance. Phytotoxicity is the capacity of a compound to cause damage to plants, which may be temporary or long-lasting and may extend to unintended plant species due to impurities or contaminants. A proposer is any manufacturer or interested party submitting a draft specification and data package to FAO/WHO for evaluation. The reference specification serves as the primary criterion for determining equivalence of technical-grade active ingredients or formulations from different manufacturers. The reference profile includes the purity/impurity, toxicological, and ecotoxicological profiles upon which the original specification is based. It is used to assess equivalence but is not amended by data from additional equivalent materials. Sedimentation refers to the settling of particles in a liquid medium. Sieving separates particles by size using sieves. Size distribution describes the mass or numerical frequency of particles in a material, while size range defines the upper and lower size limits. A specification outlines the parameters and criteria defining the physical and chemical properties of pesticides, linked to hazard and risk profiles. FAO and WHO specifications are published alongside evaluation reports on their respective websites. A subsequent manufacturer is any pesticide manufacturer other than the original proposer of a specification. A surfactant is a formulant that reduces interfacial tension, enhancing emulsifying, spreading, dispersibility, or wetting properties. Tolerance refers to permitted limits of variation in active ingredient content. Toxicity is the inherent property of an agent to cause adverse biological effects. Undersize particles are smaller than a specified size, while oversize particles exceed a specified size. Non-flammable materials have a flash point above 55°C. The glossary also includes definitions of various pesticide formulations, such as emulsifiable concentrates, suspension concentrates, and water-soluble granules, each designed for specific applications and modes of action.
